name: feature-envy
intent: Records what Feature Envy costs: a method that spends more of its time reaching into another object's data than into its own — so the knowledge of how that data is used stays in the wrong class, and every rule touching it has to be edited there instead of beside the data.
problem: A method lives in class A but operates almost entirely on an object of class B: it calls half a dozen getters on B to compute a value, or reaches through B into C to reach D. The knowledge about how B's data is used now sits in A, while B cannot enforce or reuse any of it.
context: The canonical case, in Fowler and Beck's words, is a function that spends more time communicating with functions or data inside another module than it does within its own module — most often invoking a string of getters on another object to calculate a value. It is also extremely common among clients of data classes, and it frequently appears after fields are moved to a data class while the operations on those fields are left behind. The rule the smell breaks is 'put things together that change together': data and the behaviour that references that data usually change together, and moving the behaviour elsewhere splits them.
benefits: Knowledge sits with the data: when the rule for using those fields changes, it changes in the class that owns the fields, and every caller benefits at once.
Duplication disappears. The same sequence of getters-and-arithmetic written in three clients is one method on the data class.
Invariants become enforceable. Once the arithmetic lives next to the data, the data class can refuse to be constructed in the inconsistent state that the callers kept assuming away.
Client classes shrink to what they are actually for, which is usually coordination — and their tests shrink with them.
tradeoffs: Moving the method is not always free: the moved method often needs the original class's context, so it gains parameters it did not have, and its old caller may end up with a thinner reason to exist.

The heuristic is genuinely ambiguous when a method uses features of several classes. Fowler and Beck's rule is to ask which class holds most of the data — but that is a judgement call, not a measurement.

Some designs pull behaviour away from the data on purpose. Strategy and Visitor exist to make behaviour independently changeable; Move Method applied there puts together things that were deliberately kept apart, and the price is indirection.
Over-correcting turns a cohesive client into a bag of delegating methods. A method that is a pure forwarder after the move is now a middle man.

Behaviour that is genuinely about the client — 'how this screen renders a record', 'how this workflow steps through a record' — belongs in the client, and envy of a value object's fields is not automatically a smell.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the codebase while the smell is present. Feature Envy is a structural smell, not a runtime one: performance and scalability stay high because a method that reads another object's fields is in-process work with no cost of its own. Maintainability, extensibility and discoverability are the axes that suffer, because the knowledge is filed under the wrong class; coupling is low in absolute terms but points the wrong way — the client reaches deeper into its collaborator than the client itself.

participants.responsibility: Computes a value or performs a decision almost entirely from another object's data, while contributing little of its own class's state to the computation.
participants.notes: If only part of the method is envious, Extract Method first and move only the jealous part.

participants.responsibility: Owns the data being manipulated, and currently exposes enough of it (getters, public fields) for the method to do the work.
participants.notes: It cannot enforce an invariant or reuse the arithmetic, because it does not know the rule exists.

participants.responsibility: Repeat the same manipulation, which is how you notice the duplication that betrays the envy.
participants.notes: Several clients doing the same thing to the same object is the usual smell signal.

use_cases: A `RecordPlayer` that reads `record.getGenre()`, `record.getName()` and `record.getDuration()` to format a display string, when the formatting is a property of the record.
A report generator that reaches through a `Machine` object into its fields to build the report text — the Refactoring Workbook's own Exercise 34 example.
An ORM entity that has been stripped down to fields while the business rules on those fields stayed in the service layer that reads them.
Repeated `date.getYear() * 12 + date.getMonth()` arithmetic copied into three calendar helpers instead of living on a value object.
Validation logic in a controller that inspects five fields of an incoming DTO one rule at a time.
avoid_when: The behaviour is deliberately separated from the data for independent changeability — Strategy, Visitor or a policy object placed there on purpose; move it back and you re-create the Divergent Change those patterns exist to prevent.
The method is fundamentally about the client. A view-model or presenter that formats a domain object for display is envious of its data by job description.

The 'data' is a third-party or framework type you cannot extend — move the operation to your own wrapper and leave the caller's intent intact, or use an extension/adapter rather than pretending the rule belongs to the foreign type.
The language has no way to attach the operation to the type — a plain struct-of-arrays in a numeric kernel, where the 'class' owns no data at all and functions operating on it are the right shape.
The method is a single short accessor wrapper, where the indirection would cost more than it saves.
pitfalls: Moving a method that needs three parameters it did not have before; if the moved method needs a reference back to the client, the envy was not the real problem.
Repeatedly fixing one envious method and leaving the class just as coupled, because the rule was really a cross-cutting concern rather than a data operation.
Extracting the arithmetic into a static helper instead of onto the data class, which relocates the envy rather than removing it.
Mistaking 'this method calls many methods' for envy — a method that is genuinely a coordinator legitimately touches several collaborators; envy is about whose *data* dominates.

related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy separates behaviour from the data on purpose, to make the varying part independently changeable; that is the sanctioned reason for a method not sitting beside its data, and the main contraindication to moving an envious method.
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Visitor is the same deliberate split expressed as a type dispatch: the operations live outside the visited types by construction, so feature envy there is intended rather than accidental.
related_patterns_notes.value-object: A value object is the usual destination for the moved method: once the arithmetic or rule lands on the type that owns the data, it can be a value object with its own equals, invariants and reuse.
related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: A data mapper is the deliberate inverse position — the mapper knows how to move data between a domain object and a record without owning domain rules; that boundary exists precisely so the rules stay on the domain side.
related_patterns_notes.collecting-parameter: When the envious method is really a long list of arguments threaded through a call chain, collecting them into a parameter object is the same move at the signature level.

anti_patterns: The getter fan-out: a method whose body is mostly `other.getX()` calls computing a value that plainly belongs to `other`.
Data class plus rule-shaped clients: a class stripped to fields, with every invariant enforced (if at all) by whichever client happens to check it.
Reaching through one object to get at a third: `a.getB().getC()` inside a method of a class that has no business knowing about B or C.
Duplicated arithmetic that hides in several clients, so no single place shows the whole rule.
The 'just move it back' reflex: applying Move Method where behaviour was intentionally split out by Strategy or Visitor, undoing that split for symmetry.
Moving the envy into a `Utils` function that takes the object as a parameter — the knowledge is still outside the data's class, now with an extra hop.
design_principles: Information expert: the class that holds the data knows the most about it and is the right home for the operations over that data.
Tell, don't ask: rather than reaching into another object's fields and computing a decision in the client, ask the data to compute it.
Encapsulation: getters that hand out raw fields are what make the envy possible; invariants cannot be enforced through them.
Put things together that change together: data and the behaviour referencing it usually change in the same commit — a heuristic with stated exceptions.
High cohesion: cohesion is measured inside a class, and feature envy is the measurable symptom of cohesion that got misplaced.
best_practices: Look for the duplication, not the method: several clients performing the same manipulation of one object is the cheapest reliable signal.
Count references, not intuition — an envious method typically reads more distinct fields/methods of another type than of its own; that count is checkable in review and in static analysis.
Extract Method on the jealous part first, then Move Method; moving a whole method that is only partly envious drags the rest of it across for no reason.
Move the fields too when the class is a pure data class — the refactoring notebook's diagnosis is that the smell often follows the extraction of fields, so the operations should follow them out.
When the data is in a record or a map rather than a class, the destination is a function that takes the record and returns a value — the same rule in functional dress.
Check for a legitimate reason first: DAOs, mappers, serializers and Strategy implementations are all envious by design and must be left alone.
After the move, re-check the old class: if it is now a set of pure delegations, inline it.
sources: Kent Beck, 'Smells to Refactorings' / Martin Fowler, 'Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code' (Addison-Wesley, 1999), 'Feature Envy' — the 'put things together that change together' heuristic and the Strategy/Visitor exception: https://www.informit.com/articles/article.aspx?p=2952392&seqNum=9
